# Putting Customers First: How NatWest Uses AI to Resolve Complaints Faster


[NatWest Group](https://medium.com/@NatWestGroup?source=post_page---byline--6d40de80f3eb-----------------------------------------)


9 min read


·


2 hours ago


--


*by*[Conor Hamill (Senior Data Scientist)](https://www.linkedin.com/in/conor-hamill/)


## TL;DR


**The Challenge:** NatWest case handlers spend too much time manually digging through fragmented data (calls, transactions, logs) to investigate customer complaints, slowing down resolution times.


**The Solution:** We developed the **Complaint Investigation Assistant** , an AI agent powered by the latest technology. Unlike standard chatbots, this agent can actively use “data tools” to search across multiple systems, summarize events, and provide a chronological audit trail.


**The Human Element:** This is a “human-in-the-loop” tool. The AI organizes and drafts the evidence, but the trained professional remains in full control of the final decision and ensures a fair outcome.


**The Result:** Initial deployment shows significant time savings for handlers, improved consistency, and high marks for accuracy and ethical safety. The methodology behind our Complaint Investigation Assistant was[recently accepted and presented at the EMNLP 2026 conference Industry Track](https://aclanthology.org/2026.emnlp-industry.227/) , where it was awarded runner-up for best paper.


This external recognition reinforces that we’re not only building tools that help colleagues and customers today, but also contributing rigorous and innovative applications of AI back to the wider community.


## The Challenge


Whenever you’ve raised a complaint with your bank, you don’t want them spending time digging through your information to understand what’s happened — **you want it sorted as quickly and as reliably as possible** . But resolving a customer’s complaint is complex and challenging; there are many back-end systems and since customers can get in touch about any service NatWest offers (everyday spending, getting a mortgage, saving for the future), there’s a wide variety of cases to address. This means that often case handlers **spend a lot of their time navigating different systems** to piece together a full picture of what happened, when they could be directly supporting the customer and getting to the bottom of their complaint.


Recent research from NatWest[shared at the ACL 2026 conference](https://openreview.net/forum?id=KfcWaTdGVi) has highlighted how **AI can assist handlers in complex customer support tasks** by identifying the reason for their call. To solve this, we have recently launched Complaint Investigation Assistant, an AI agent that reads a customer complaint and intelligently searches through a range of data systems to provide the case handler with its summary of events.


Crucially, the agent is designed from the ground up as **a “human-in-the-loop” tool: it supports case handlers in their work,** but the handler remains in control and is ultimately responsible for ensuring a fair outcome is given and documented.


This has been achieved by building on our previous work where we enhanced the complaint handler journey by developing a[tool that uses GenAI to draft regulation-compliant letters](https://openreview.net/forum?id=Ugq9awukHx) . These initiatives are accelerated by[NatWest’s collaboration with OpenAI](https://www.natwestgroup.com/news-and-insights/latest-stories/ai-and-data/2025/mar/accelerating-our-ai-transformation-in-banking-with-openai.html) and supported by our[AI Ethics Code of Conduct](https://www.natwestgroup.com/sustainability/society/innovation-and-digitisation.html) .


## Technical solution


The development of AI agents has been a major advancement in Generative AI ([recent review](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5381584) ). Anthropic[define an AI agent](https://www.anthropic.com/research/measuring-agent-autonomy) as “an AI system equipped with tools that allow it to take actions, like running code, calling external APIs, and sending messages to other agents”.


> The ability \[of AI agents\] to take step-by-step actions and use tools has opened up a wide range of tasks that previously weren’t possible with static LLMs.


### High level approach


Press enter or click to view image in full size


AI Investigation Agent with data tools, generated using OpenAI’s GPT Image model.


Our agent system consists of a single AI agent with read-only access to a range of data systems via a library of data tools that we developed. The core LLM is from OpenAI’s GPT family, chosen after experimentation with different LLMs and agent setups for its intelligence, adherence to instructions, and very long context window, meaning it can read and refer to a large amount of source data in a single run.


We tested multi-agent and alternative model approaches, but a single GPT-based agent with carefully designed tools and prompts struck the best balance between quality, controllability, and simplicity. We developed the agent using the[OpenAI Agents SDK](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/) , which provided a clear API and constrained execution to only the tools we defined.


These data tools provide access to a range of data systems, including customer call transcripts, account transactions, and an internal knowledge base. The AI agent is able to call these data tools, which return the data to the agent and append it to its context window. For the data tool connected to an internal knowledge base, the agent is able to provide its own queries, enabling dynamic searching of guidance that is relevant to insights found in other data sources. For example, if one source shows a customer asking about a specific bank process, the AI agent can use another tool to search for guidance on that same process. **This adaptiveness from the step-by-step tool use allows the AI agent to produce rich and relevant outputs** .

A key design principle is that the agent is constrained to only cite information returned by its tools — it cannot draw on its general training knowledge for complaint-specific claims. **This grounding mechanism, combined with the chronological evidence trail in the detailed description, gives handlers a clear audit path to verify every statement** . When a tool call fails — for example if a system is unavailable — the agent reports this transparently rather than attempting to infer the missing information, a deliberate design choice to prevent hallucination.


> This pattern, co-designed with the business, helps ensure that the agent tools are built around real needs, tested thoroughly, and deployed in a way that colleagues can trust.


Whenever the AI agent is called, it reads in the description of the customer complaint and then calls the data tools in turn, until it has determined that it has enough information to write a summary of the investigation. The output from the agent, **which is presented to the case handler for review** , consists of two components: a summary and detailed description. The summary is a long paragraph that gives an overall description of the background of the customer complaint, while the detailed description is a chronological list of events that helped to inform the summary, with the date, reference number, and system that information was taken from.

### How we designed it for the case handlers to do their job well


The output from the AI agent was designed to give the case handlers the ability to rapidly understand the background of the complaint, with the option to explore and verify specific events in more detail. Reporting a comprehensive view of the tool usage also helped to understand what systems the agent has and hasn’t queried, allowing the handlers to add supplementary information if required.


> **Having a human in the loop is a key part of the system** ; the case handler is able to edit and append to the draft investigation notes and, as before this system was deployed, is responsible for the accuracy of the details within. For customers, this means that an AI system is never making decisions on its own — it is organising information and drafting text, but a trained professional, with context and judgement, is always the one deciding what happens next.


NatWest case handlers bring deep, niche expertise to these investigations — expertise that is not captured in any base LLM. They understand the nuances of NatWest products, processes, regulatory obligations, and the lived realities of customers in a way that a general-purpose model does not. The agent is designed to surface relevant information quickly so that handlers can apply that expertise more effectively, not to replace them.


### Evaluation and validation


Across the GenAI projects, data scientists in NatWest use a combination of SME assessment and LLM-as-a-judge evaluation. LLM-as-a-judge is a method that uses another LLM to grade the quality of the output of the model, similar to previous works on automating the[drafting of complaint final response letters](https://openreview.net/forum?id=Ugq9awukHx) and[enhancing our internal support chatbot AskArchie](https://nwg.ai/from-rag-to-riches-evaluating-systems-and-their-components-7dea97380fcd?source=collection_home_page----6077d4d39315-----7-----------------------------------) . This dual evaluation approach gives a mix of expert assessment and rapid feedback for quick prompt and system design iteration.


We measured the quality of the output of the AI agent across a range of metrics, including the relevancy and accuracy of the output, whether it provided the handler with a complete background of the customer complaint, and the clarity of the writing. Evaluation by case handlers on the quality of the output found that the output met or exceeded the success criteria across all of these metrics.


In production, the monitoring of the model is done using a combination of the LLM-as-a-judge method, which is run for every single agent output, and human evaluation, with case handlers being asked for feedback on the agent output frequently. This ensures that any changes to the quality of the model output are detected and rectified as soon as possible.


### Bias and fairness


One of NatWest’s AI principles is that AI systems “are free from bias and discrimination”; to ensure this, **we measured the quality of the output across different customer demographics and found no statistical difference in model performance** , indicating that the model does not favour one group of customers over another.[Research undertaken in NatWest has shown](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.16989) that the removal of explicit demographic markers does not necessarily remove all biases in LLMs when culturally indicative names remain, making empirical evaluation across demographics and ongoing monitoring in production essential.


An extensive report on the model design and evaluation was submitted to and reviewed by the internal independent model risk team. Alongside this, the system was reviewed by the internal Data & AI Ethics panel, who deemed it not a high-risk product launch. All AI use cases are triaged by this panel, with panels assessing use cases for their alignment with the bank’s[AI Ethics Code of Conduct](https://www.natwestgroup.com/sustainability/society/innovation-and-digitisation.html) . In production, every agent output is automatically assessed for bias as part of our LLM-as-a-judge monitoring pipeline, ensuring any emerging patterns are caught early.


NatWest’s collaboration with OpenAI, which was[launched last year](https://www.natwestgroup.com/news-and-insights/latest-stories/ai-and-data/2025/mar/accelerating-our-ai-transformation-in-banking-with-openai.html) , was a key part of this project. Regular sessions with experts from OpenAI allowed us to have a deep dive into our approaches for developing and evaluating the model, ensuring that we were following best practices with this rapidly evolving technology, and giving us the confidence that the tool we were developing is accurate and robust.


## Launching Complaint Investigation Assistant


Complaint Investigation Assistant has now been **launched across many teams inside NatWest Group** , with each team being given training on what the tool is, how it can assist them in their role, what its limitations are, and the critical role they continue to play in reviewing the output and delivering fair outcomes for customers. Initial feedback has been very positive, with handlers using the tool on the day it was launched commenting how much time they’ve saved from not having to search through systems for key information. We are expecting the adoption of the tool across teams to improve the speed and quality of the responses to customer complaints.


## Next steps


This first phase of Complaint Investigation Assistant was limited to the most common complaint categories and most frequently used systems by case handlers; this was an intentional decision to deploy the tool with core capabilities, rather than pushing back the launch to include more categories and systems. The next phase will expand the number of complaint categories and data systems, meaning more customers and colleagues will be able to benefit from the investigation agent.


> The number one piece of feedback we’ve got from handlers is that they want further systems added so that they can get even more benefit out of this AI agent tool.


This work builds on our past experience in deploying Generative AI tools in the bank. This investigation agent marks the team’s first deployment of an AI agent, and one of the first AI agents in the bank, alongside our new agentic financial assistant within[Cora](https://www.natwestgroup.com/news-and-insights/latest-stories/ai-and-data/2026/feb/being-a-trusted-partner-for-tomorrows-banking-through-technology.html) . We have developed a pattern of giving an AI agent access to many data tools to allow it to intelligently investigate a complaint, and we believe this has the potential to be applied in many other use cases in the bank.


## Conclusion


Generative AI has rapidly changed many industries, including financial services, and has improved customer and colleague experiences across a range of use cases in NatWest Group, including[customer correspondence](https://openreview.net/forum?id=Ugq9awukHx) ,[internal knowledge base retrieval](https://nwg.ai/from-rag-to-riches-evaluating-systems-and-their-components-7dea97380fcd?source=collection_home_page----6077d4d39315-----7-----------------------------------) , and[customer support](https://www.natwestgroup.com/news-and-insights/latest-stories/ai-and-data/2026/feb/being-a-trusted-partner-for-tomorrows-banking-through-technology.html) . AI agents are also quickly changing how work is done, with their ability to intelligently use tools and comprehend a large amount of unstructured data opening up many use cases.


With the launch of Complaint Investigation Assistant, we have provided case handlers with a tool that presents a summary of the background of a customer complaint, enabling them to understand the case much more quickly, reducing cognitive load from switching between multiple systems, and meaning they can spend more of their time directly supporting customers. Extensive model validation and review by the internal independent model risk team and the Data & AI Ethics panel has given us confidence that the model is aligned with NatWest’s Data Ethics and AI principles. Initial feedback from case handlers using the tool has been positive, with excitement that the next phase of the investigation agent will involve expanding it to more categories and data systems.


As LLMs and AI agents become more powerful, the complexity of tasks they can undertake reliably[continues to grow rapidly](https://metr.org/time-horizons/) . We see the pattern developed in Complaint Investigation Assistant with an AI agent that can access data sources through data tools as applicable across many areas in the bank and see further work with AI agents as a chance to simplify processes and improve experiences for customers and colleagues.
